utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are present. I see all the Defence teams present here, with some new faces. We will come to that very soon. And Prosecution, it's just Mr. McCloskey this morning. So, Mr. Zivanovic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I just like to introduce our new legal assistant, Filippo de Minicis, he is sitting with us today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Filippo -- could you repeat the surname, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Filippo de Minicis. Mr. DE MINICIS: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. My name is Filippo de Minicis, legal assistant for Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You are most welcome. I also notice a new arrival as co-counsel in the Borovcanin Defence team. Mr. Gosnell, on behalf of the Trial Chamber I wish to welcome you. This is a kind of system rather which is quite different from what you are used to at home. You will get used to it as we go along. I'm sure you have been sufficiently briefed on how we operate here. But I'm sure that you will find your way without much ado. I also notice a new face in the Pandurevic team, even if it's behind the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, that's Ms. Kinga Tibori. She is a legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. So I think we can start. But before we start, I think we owe a tribute to your predecessor, Mr. Gosnell, Mr. Miodrag Stojanovic. He's been with us here since the beginning of the case. He was counsel here, lead counsel, in another case. He's a very capable lawyer who distinguished himself in more ways than one. He was capable, he prepared his case on a daily basis. He was courteous towards the Trial Chamber and to his colleagues both on the Defence and the Prosecution side. He did a great job together with Mr. Lazarevic. And we are thankful for his services. We will miss him and we ask you, Mr. Lazarevic, to convey to him our best wishes for whatever lies ahead in his career which so far has been brilliant enough. Thank you. So the reason why we are convened here today is the outcome of the filings that took place pursuant to Rule 65 ter(G), and also because we felt that pursuant to Rule 73 ter, we should exercise our discretion to hold a Pre-Defence Conference. In preparation for this Pre-Defence Conference, we asked our Senior Legal Officer, Mr. Cubbon, to convene and preside over a 65 ter meeting with you, with a view to preparing better the various Defence cases that we have scheduled for the coming months. I wish to thank you all for attending the 65 ter meeting although there were some shortcomings that could have been avoided but which I will avoid going into, and I also wish to thank Mr. Cubbon for having conducted the meeting in such an admirable manner. We went through the transcript of the meeting, and we also had a very detailed report by Mr. Cubbon or from Mr. Cubbon, which puts us in a position to take up the issue of the preparation of the Defence case where it was left at the end of the 65 ter meeting. There are some matters that are not going to be discussed, but which need to be recorded. First thing is we asked and we are informed that Mr. Cubbon did inform you that one of the expert witnesses, some of you intend to offer, whether he will be accepted is another matter of course, is Professor William Schabas and we wanted you to know that Professor Schabas is and has been a very close personal friend of mine and of Judge Prost for a long number of years, not that it mattered much to us, but we wanted you to know about this. We understand that this has been brought to your attention, both Defence teams and interested Defence teams and Prosecution, and that according to you, there is nothing that you wish to state on the matter. In other words, that no further action is needed. That is what we have been told. So I'm just putting this down in the record and for the record. Now the main purpose of the 65 ter meeting, and of course this Pre-Defence Conference is, as I have already said, the planning of the remainder of the trial. In introducing the subject, I refer you to Rule 73 ter with the title Pre-Defence Conference, which inter alia empowers the Trial Chamber to call upon the Defence to shorten the estimated length of the examination-in-chief for some witnesses, empowers equally the Trial Chamber, after hearing submissions from the Defence, to set the number of witnesses the Defence may call. And last, but not least, authorises the Trial Chamber to determine the time available to the Defence for presenting evidence. I'm mentioning all this not because we have in our mind decided in one way or another to put into effect any of these three measures. As you will recall, our approach from the beginning of the trial has been that if you are reasonable, we will endeavour to be even more reasonable, and in that manner try to move ahead and achieve the greatest efficiency. We gave it a try. And having done our homework, we considered the following. We considered that during the Prosecution case, the Prosecution used 266 hours, we used very little time and mostly in disposing of procedural matters, and the seven Defence teams altogether used 413 hours, which is 48 per cent of the total sitting time. We were aware of this when earlier on in the year, after hearing your submissions, we decided that it was reasonable to grant you three months for the preparation of the various Defence cases. We did so for two reasons, mainly. One of the reasons is that this is indeed a very complicated and complex case involving serious crimes and involving perhaps one of the most significant events in the history of the war in ex-Yugoslavia, and we felt that adequate time was necessary to that extent for a proper preparation of the Defence, but it could also have been shorter. Why didn't we fix a shorter time? Because we were led by you all, I would say, I wouldn't distinguish between one and the other, to believe that this will not be labour lost; this will be a useful exercise which would ultimately translate in a Defence case which would be shorter and reasonably shorter than what we would otherwise -- what one would otherwise expect. And these were our expectations. Now, I must confess, and this is not just my opinion but the opinion of everyone here, that we do appreciate the effort made by some of you in doing their utmost to limit the length of the Defence -- of their Defence case. But we are still concerned that we haven't reached the optimum or what we had expected. In preparation for the 65 ter meeting, we discussed this with our Senior Legal Officer and we gave him strict instructions to discuss the matter of the expected length of Defence cases with you, communicate to you our concerns, and invite you to consider possible reductions in your Defence case, respective Defence cases. He reported back to us and today this will constitute one of the most important, perhaps the focal, issue of the Pre-Defence Conference. The way we are going to proceed now is a very simple one. I am not going to recall or repeat what was discussed during the 65 ter conference because that is common knowledge, but I am going to call on each one of you to inform the Trial Chamber if you have considered areas where you think reductions on your part are possible. At the end of this exercise, we will take stock of the situation, after which we will take a decision. At the present moment, as I said, we have no plans at all to take one rather than another decision. That very much depends on what will be the outcome of the discussions today. We are going to start with the Beara Defence team and we are going to start with the Beara Defence team not because we want to single the accused Beara -- single out the accused Beara, but it's because we consider, having gone through the details of the filings by the Beara Defence team, that the anticipated or the suggested Defence case by that team is excessive, when it comes to time needed for its completion. Some information was exchanged during the 65 ter meeting, and what we would like to know from the Beara Defence team now is whether there are any intentions on your part to put in place any reductions in your Defence case. Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning. Yes, we've discussed that briefly among our team members and I also spoke to the Court Senior Legal Officer and we have indicated that we will make some reductions. We don't know exactly if the Court will consider them to be significant but we will consult with our client this afternoon and tomorrow and I've also invited the Prosecution to sit down with us tomorrow, all day if necessary, in order to meet some of the Court's guidelines on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's too vague.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is the Court looking for a specific number from us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What the Court is looking for is concrete information, Mr. Ostojic. It's already the second time, during the 65 ter meeting we got nothing out of Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry that the Court feels that and I can tell the Court that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we got nothing out of Mr. Meek and the main reason being probably that you were not present and we are getting nothing out of you or almost nothing out of you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry the Court feels that way. I'm being very sincere with the Court when I said that we looked at all the witnesses again, we will pare it down, I can't give the Court a specific number without consulting with my client. He was yesterday with a family visit all day and the last several days. I think we can pare it down by 20 per cent, if the Court wants me to make a guesstimate but that obviously, Mr. President, depends on many factors such as the Court's ruling on the 92 bis suggestions that we made. If in my meeting with the Prosecution they are able to agree that certain witnesses can be brought in under Rule 92 bis, certainly we will remove them. We think there is some duplication. I don't think that it's more than 20 per cent. We think it's necessary to show some of the facts and I did hear the Court's message on some of the pre-1995 issues but, with all due respect, I think it's necessary in light of the Court's most recent ruling where they suggested that pattern, conduct and intent for crimes subsequent to the dates that are in the indictment are indeed relevant and I think that those in 92 which we will draw upon but ever so briefly for the Court are important and relevant in this case. I can assure the Court we are working vigorously to reduce the list and I can tell you that right now from my best guesstimate I can say that I would suggest that there would be a 20 to 25 per cent cut from the original list but do I have to check with all team members and Mr. Beara as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let us put one thing clear for the record, Mr. Meek, that our intervention in all this and our part in all this is in no way related to whether any witness or piece of evidence that you intend to bring forward is relevant or not. We are in no way telling you eliminate what is not relevant because we are not prepared to tell you whether a piece of evidence is relevant now as things stand. That is your responsibility and we'll deal with it as we go along. So the position is as follows: There is a validity and a lot of sense in what you've just said in relation to outstanding possible Rule 92 bis and Rule 92 ter witnesses. And those are pleasures yet to come. We'll still need to receive feedback from the Prosecution on the various motions that have been filed. I am not sure if you have filed your motion on Rule 92 bis and 92 ter. I don't recall having seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I believe we have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have? Okay. So what we will expect is an answer, a reply, from Mr. McCloskey, and that should put us in a position not only in relation, in regard your client but also in relation to the other Defence teams, what the position is, because there are various Defence teams that have asked for witnesses to be heard via the Rule 92 bis and 92 ter procedure. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, the last thing having heard what you plan doing after consultations with your colleagues and also with Mr. McCloskey, is we would like you to state here when you expect to be in a position to give a concrete answer to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm confident I can do that by the end of business tomorrow, Your Honour, if the Prosecution is available to meet with me tomorrow, I'm available all day to meet with him and willing to meet with him and I'm quite confident that we will be able to resolve most of the issues to give you that exact answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. That's reasonable, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we work very well with the Beara team. We only need the 92 bis statements for that to work and I know they know that and so if that is coming, we will be able to manage that rather quickly but we do need those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I meant when I hadn't seen them actually, but -- Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When will you be in a position to provide the Prosecution with the 92 bis statements? Even in draft form?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Judge Kwon. We don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because you had a time limit to do that and that passed already and you haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we typically don't get the signed statements from the witnesses and I will give him everything we have including some of my notes so long as it's not privileged in my opinion. I may even share that with him because I'm confident that he's not going to divulge it but I think he'll be reasonably satisfied that he'll have more than enough information. And for the record if I may just point out from my opinion, I think our summaries were quite extensive and should have provided adequate or more than adequate information to the Prosecution and that they were able to at least make an estimate as to how long each of those witnesses may potentially be cross-examined, but I will however continue to endeavour to provide him all the information that we have within the Rules so that he can be fully satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's clarify this because as I'm sure you know, Mr. Ostojic, that for the purpose of Rule 92 bis or 92 ter for that matter, what is required from you to provide the Prosecution or the other party is not witness summaries, it's the full statement of that or those witnesses. And that is what is missing. So what you are required and what Mr. McCloskey will certainly expect from you before he can make a reasoned decision is the statement or statements of your witnesses and not the summaries. This is why I'm asking you whether you are in a position to provide them in good time, if you intend to come back to us with a corrected forecast of your Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I'm prepared and I'm ready to proceed with the Prosecution at his convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a possibility that you meet between today and tomorrow, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you both. Now, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Same questions to you. Your case, when we worked our calculations, also is expected to take pretty long. You have, of course, this pending question of the Prosecution reopening of its case, which probably will need to be decided by the Appeals Chamber but we'll come back to you soon on that. But forgetting that, and irrespective and independently of that, have you done any homework following the 65 ter meeting, which leads you to some possible reductions in your Defence case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we reduced our list, we shall drop one witness from the list, and we shall reduce some time for the examination-in-chief of some other witnesses. Some of the common witnesses will appear in the case of the other accused. These are Mrs. Danijela Danojlovic, Mr. Milenko Jevdjevic and our common expert, Mr. Djuro Radic. I intended to file a notice to the Chamber today or tomorrow, and you will have all details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's very kind of you, Mr. Zivanovic. Thank you. Do you wish to state anything in regard, Mr. McCloskey? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. It's more or less the same issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, we have taken into consideration -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have taken into consideration the suggestions that we were given through the Senior Legal Officer, in those areas where assistance and reduction is expected in the Nikolic Defence case. What I can say for the moment is that the Defence has decided concerning one viva voce witness related to the Zvornik hospital area, to put him on as a 92 ter witness, to reduce the time of examination. As for a group of witnesses related to year 1992, we had had a number of contacts with the Office of the Prosecutor in order to stipulate the facts that these witnesses could possibly testify about. So that in case agreement is reached, this could considerably reduce the Defence case for accused Nikolic. As for the 92 bis witness statements, we will spend next week working in the Zvornik area and we expect to be able to submit the results of this mission after that work is done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Nikolic. When you say as for the 92 bis statements -- sorry, witness statements, are you referring to Witnesses 12, 16 and 19? Or to someone else?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for 12, 16 and 19, two statements have already been attached to our 92 bis statements and the only missing statement is for the Witness 396.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure if she had the number correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which witness has a missing statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell the Chamber immediately. There are four 92 bis witnesses for whom we have not provided statements and we have informed the Chamber accordingly. Those are numbers 3 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel read them again slowly?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you read them out again slowly, please, for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. 3DV15, 3DV16, 3DV18, and 3DV27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the position as regards these four witnesses is what, if you could state it again?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The situation is that we will see these witnesses next week again and try to take statements signed by these witnesses and attach them to our 92 bis submission within the shortest time possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Madam Nikolic. Otherwise, there are no other areas where you propose reductions, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not for the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Madam. Mr. Lazarevic? Or Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for your welcome this morning. I'm going to address the Chamber briefly on this. As you know, Your Honour, from having looked at the -- our submission, of course, you'll know we are starting from a rather low base. We are proposing to call a total of 19 witnesses, two of them are joint, and of those, three will be 92 bis witnesses. So that leaves 14 of our own witnesses. Our plan is to try to, in your words, optimise the Court's time by exploring the possibility of additional 92 ter or 92 bis statements and we hope to ensure that our case is kept to an efficient scope. We will of course advise the Chamber as soon as possible, make a filing indicating when we know whether that will be a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, fair enough, Mr. Gosnell. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we can say to the Chamber that we will certainly withdraw at least two of our witnesses. For the moment I'm not in a position to say which witnesses they will be because obviously we have to make a very specific choice. Also, for witnesses 23 and 24 on our list, we are envisaging seriously to present them according to Article 92 ter of the Rules. The only thing which we will ask from the Chamber is to grant us time to prepare the statements and we will contact these witnesses and we'll make an appointment with them so we may need to have enough time to give these statements. Also, we envisage to shorten the time necessary for our examinations on direct which would reduce also the time indicated, which I think was 70 hours, so we could reduce it to about 58 hours, and of course we will explore other possibilities, possibly to present other 92 ter witnesses or to shorten certain cross-examinations. We also have seven witnesses who are common to other teams of Defence which would enable us to reduce more the time necessary because I'm sure that cross-examinations will be covered by other teams of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Incidentally, in relation to the time that you have expressed you would -- you stated you would need for the purpose of filing 92 ter motions, I mean, the idea as I understand it, will be that we will start the Defence teams according to the indictment. So it will be quite some time before your turn comes up, even if everyone shortens his Defence case, even if there is a significant reduction. But in any case, there is also a second option, that there is a beginning and an end with an intervening period of time to every Defence case, and you can, in addition, plan to have these 92 ter witnesses if the motion is granted brought forth for cross-examination towards the end of your case rather than in -- near the beginning. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case should you require the assistance of the Trial Chamber we will, as we have done in the past, provide you with it. And not just to you but to all of you. Mr. Josse, Mr. Krgovic, I don't know who is going to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were two issues that Mr. Cubbon raised at the 65 ter conference. The first relates to witnesses testifying on the roles of morale, religious and legal affairs sectors at both corps and brigade levels and how they interacted with the Main Staff. That issue we can categorically state will be one we will be able to reduce the amount of witnesses we propose to call, either by physically reducing the number or by producing 92 bis and/or 92 ter witness statements. We are, I repeat, very confident that that issue will be reduced. The other issue that the Trial Chamber brought to our attention, that is the whereabouts of General Gvero in late July of 1995, is frankly rather more problematic. Our investigation has indicated a significant number of people, up to 100, I'm told, who say they saw General Gvero at that time in the western part of Bosnia. We have already cut the list down considerably. That being said, let me make it clear our investigation has not finished in this regard and the Trial Chamber will be aware that this became a live issue in the case relatively late on and that is why the investigation is still ongoing. Mr. Krgovic and I have discussed the issue at some length following the 65 ter Conference and we are going to try and produce 92 bis and/or 92 ter witness statements for some, if not all, of the people involved. Frankly, Your Honour, we think it unlikely that 92 bis applies, although any guidance in that regard would be most gratefully received but we would have thought a suggestion by a Defence team that an accused was not where the Prosecution allege that he was must be a matter that goes to the acts and conduct of that accused and therefore not suitable for a 92 bis statement. Therefore, it's going to have to be 92 ter. What Your Honour has just said to my learned friend Madam Fauveau is something we are most delighted to hear because, frankly, we are not going to be in a position to tender those statements for a considerable period of time and bearing in mind what you've just said to her, the Trial Chamber clearly are saying that they don't need to be tendered for a considerable period of time. That being said, we can assure the Trial Chamber we will get on and do our best to produce these various statements. But it will take primarily Mr. Krgovic's own personal attention and these witnesses are spread over different parts of Bosnia so it's something he's going to have to do as this trial progresses. I hope that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. However, related to all this, and I meant to refer to this later on, but you may sit down, Mr. Josse, there is a matter of great importance that I want you to address your minds to, that planning each of the Defence cases is not only our problem. It is primarily our problem but we would like to make it clear that whoever is before you or whoever is coming after you also needs to have a clear indication of when to expect their case to come up. Let me give you an example. I mean, when I look at the filings of the Gvero Defence team, forgetting for the time being what you have more or less promised today, that you will make a serious effort, which I'm sure you will, to convert several of these viva voce witnesses into 92 bis or more probably 92 ter witnesses, irrespective of whether they are going to be 92 bis or 92 ter, there will be a significant saving on time which would expectedly reduce your Defence case but that would mean that the Pandurevic case will start earlier or would be expected to start earlier. And you should also be aware that if the one before you, and you have got four -- you've got five before you, do exactly the same thing, then what you may be playing for, I don't know which month later on this year or next year, may prove to be a wrong estimate, and you will be faced with a position where you have to start -- you would find yourself in a position where you have to start your Defence case within or much earlier than you expected, with the consequence that perhaps the Rule 92 ter statements have not yet been obtained and with the further result that the expected saving on time will be lost. So this is why we are saying planning is very important for us, but you should understand, and I'm sure you understand, that it is almost more important for you because the case is yours at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Of course, we are aware of that, and we will try and do things with as much expedition as possible. So far as Mr. Haynes's position is concerned, ironically, he and I were discussing that very subject last night, namely, clearly he would need to know how long we are going to take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- because he comes immediately after us. He'll no doubt confirm that we are in the Gvero team very aware as to how that's going to impact on the Pandurevic team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, obviously. And thank you for that because I was a little bit taken aback when you used the -- or you interpreted my words, it's not a criticism, don't misread me, that I was sort of happy with Madam Fauveau or with yourself taking as much time as you think you need for the preparation of the 92 ter statements. It could well be, and I'm saying this from experience, and fortunately, I have a longer experience than -- in trials than any of you here, it could well happen that, for example, the Popovic team anticipates so many hours and will end up with -- using one half of that, you could well end up with another Defence team reducing, as we go along, the number of witnesses. I mean, in the previous case I dealt with, for example, the number of witnesses were halved in the course of the Defence case and the Defence case took almost one fourth the time of what we had authorised and what was expected. So that was just one accused. Here we have seven. So each one of us should be expected to be prepared for this. Now, for the time being I'm only saying this because later on I will touch on a very much related subject that was not discussed during the 65 ter meeting, but which is on our mind and which again mostly based on past experience of the four of us, we are sure carries a lot of importance and we want to make sure that you are fully aware of what our intentions are. But I thank you, Mr. Josse. I take note of what you promised or you undertook to do in the forthcoming days and weeks, and we expect positive results. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Rightly or wrongly, I'm working on the assumption that I will present my case this calendar year. I don't know why but that's just the way that I read the 65 ter lists ahead of me. I'm anticipating that I will have to present my case towards the end of this year. And we are ready for that. You will know that our 65 ter list is different from many others in that it contains two very substantial witnesses, I have very much in mind the shape of my case, it will begin with one of them and end with the other. And depending upon the extent of the challenge to the principal Defence witness, I anticipate losing an awful lot of witnesses thereafter but those two witnesses are going to be substantial and they will form the body of my case. I think we began with 23 witnesses. Seven of which I think are paper witnesses. We've lost another 3 to other Defence teams. It's in hand. I know the shape of it. It will take weeks, not months, to present my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Haynes. So rounding up this part of the -- yes, Madam Fauveau? I apologise to you. I didn't see you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, excuse me, I would simply give a few corrections to the notes. Page 15, lines 1 and 3, what I meant and I think everybody understood me, but just to be sure that everything is clear, it's not cross-examinations but direct examinations, which we will make an effort to shorten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The rest doesn't depend on you, Madam Fauveau. Thanks, so I would round up this first part of the discussions today and basically the position is this: Ultimately what will be decided by the Trial Chamber, because the decision will need to be taken in any case, will depend on the revised estimates that we expect from you and which you promise, some of which I suppose you are already ready, in a position to provide us with. Others will probably require a little bit more time. But we enjoin you to put us in the picture as early as possible, and this will be to your benefit. It's not just to our benefit. It's mainly to your benefit. The other obviously caveat depends on the ultimate decisions that will need to be taken in relation to applications for witnesses to be heard under Rules 92 bis or 92 ter, possibly 92 quater and we are not prepared to anticipate anything there because all depends on documents that apparently some of which have not yet been provided, and of course, we will need to await the -- to hear what the position of the Prosecution is in regard. And that again can affect on the ultimate decision that we will take. Also, in relation -- we will start with the Popovic Defence case first, so in the case of Popovic, these particular issues need to be determined the earliest possible. Don't forget that on the 2nd of June we start again, and we have to have a very clear position as to how long that case is going to take, not only because we need to know but also because the Beara team needs to know and the rest of you need to know because your cases will come up pretty soon. So rounding this up, we will await for further information, and following which we should be in a position to hand down the appropriate rulings or decisions, part of which will need to be immediately before we start with the Popovic Defence team. I am going to move on to another subject, which was touched upon during the 65 ter meeting and following which we were given the relative information by Mr. Cubbon. And that's opening statements. Now, the position as we know it until now is that the -- Mr. Zivanovic intends and requests 45 minutes for an opening statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That Mr. Ostojic also requests the opportunity to make an opening statement, but Mr. Meek was not in a position to tell us what time will be required.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No more than one hour and 30 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the Nikolic Defence team gave an indication that no -- there is no intention to have -- make an opening statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Borovcanin Defence team was not in a position to indicate the time needed for an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, at this stage I really -- it's very hard to make an estimation. I believe it won't last more than one and a half hours but I really cannot say this at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Miletic, same?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I think it's pure speculation to make an estimate. I'd prefer for the moment not to make an estimation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Gvero Defence team indicated one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's an approximation, Your Honour, but yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Pandurevic, no intention to make an opening statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: A bit early to say, but unlikely that I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, without committing ourselves to the time that you will be allotted or allocated for the opening statements, there is one problem, and that arises in relation to the -- or in the wake of the request made by the Beara team, the Beara Defence team. I will refer you, Mr. Ostojic, to Rule 84 with which I am sure you are very familiar and our recollection, our recollection I can assure you it is correct, is that when we started this case, you opted to make an opening statement which you did, and it seems to us that what the Rule states is that you have an option, you can make it then or you can make it later but you have no right to make two statements. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I read the rule actually and I respectfully disagree with the Court if that's the Court's position. It doesn't give me an option. It doesn't exclude me specifically and expressly from giving an opening statement at the commencement of my Defence case. I think it's a reasonable request, I think the time that I've stated is reasonable. I think it might be necessary for the Court in order for us to be able to summarise in a nutshell what our evidence will be, at that time we didn't have much of that evidence. Prosecution certainly from time to time has amended their witnesses and some of the theories in their case. I think the Rules do not prohibit me respectfully from presenting an opening statement before my Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, can you show us where the Rule does not prohibit you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Specifically the Rule, Your Honour, does not say that you have only one option and you can expect to either have an opening at the beginning of the trial or at the beginning of your Defence case. I do not read the Rule that way. I've looked for the decisional authority on that. I did not find some. Respectfully, I think that's a narrow reading and approach to the Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, do you have -- do you take a position on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I think the Rules are very clear about that and only one opening statement. However, I don't object to a short opening statement, especially Mr. Ostojic likes to talk about me a lot and that's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Our position on this is going to be determined now, Mr. Ostojic and Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Ostojic, you will be allowed to make an opening statement only if you show good cause. You will be asked to show this good cause when your Defence case comes up. We'll determine then whether you have shown a sufficient good cause and we will also determine the time that you will have available for your opening statement, if that is granted. Now as regards I just want for the record to confirm the position as it has been communicated to us by Mr. Cubbon. We have been indicated that -- there is no intention, at least for the time being, that Mr. Popovic or Mr. Beara make a statement of their own. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Beara? Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I don't seem to have a definitive answer as regards Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. This is a matter which is still very much under consideration and at this time I can say that Mr. Nikolic -- there is a possibility for either a statement or testimony on his behalf. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that information, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Borovcanin and Mr. -- and General Miletic, I take it that none of them wish to make a statement? Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's quite possible my client will not make a statement but maybe -- it's much too early. It's most probable that he won't make a statement, such a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Our position is very much the same as Madam Fauveau's. It is unlikely but I cannot exclude anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And now we come to you, General Gvero. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate that General Gvero unlike any of the other accused in this case did elect to make a Rule 84 bis statement prior to the commencement of the trial or presentation of evidence perhaps I should say. The way I would invite the Trial Chamber to leave this is the way they have with the opening statement so far as the Beara case is concerned. Basically, review the situation as and when it arises and that allow us to make an application and if good cause is shown, to consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Our concern, if you can call it a concern, because it's not a concern actually but General Gvero already made a statement at the beginning of the trial, and we followed that statement with great attention and giving it all due importance. And he is indicated as giving evidence later on. So obviously the question arises, if he's going to give evidence, why should he elect to make an unsworn statement before? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I give this? Could I have a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We can give a categorical assurance that it will only be one or the other. If we ask leave for a further 84 bis statement, he will not give evidence from the witness box.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. That makes more sense. That makes more sense obviously because obviously you would have asked the same question, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why should he make a statement at 9.00 in the morning lasting maybe 15 minutes or 20 minutes and then at 9.20 he starts giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no secret about this. He is on the list as one of our witnesses because he may gave evidence on his own behalf. That decision will not finally be made until the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. I appreciate that, Mr. Josse. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, this is a rather serious issue for us. So as this decision is made I'm sure counsel will tell me because should he elect to try to make another statement we would be insisting in a motion that we cross-examine him, that we be able to ask him questions about that. Of course, that's not a problem if he testifies, but if he -- we will be insisting to cross-examine him if he gets the second bite at the apple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that, I think, disposes of the issues of opening statements. The next item on my agenda is the order in which the Defence cases are to be presented, and I'm stating this just for the record. According to the report that I have from Mr. Cubbon, which I'm sure you will confirm, at the 65 ter meeting it was confirmed by the various Defence teams that they would be presenting their evidence in the order in which the accused are listed in the indictment. The consequence of that is that the Popovic Defence team will go first and he will be followed according to the list of the accused in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now we are again coming to some very serious business, starting with one aspect of it which is not very serious but which will lead to various questions, and this is the point that I was trying to make earlier on when I said that I will come back to you and try to alert you to big problems that we can foresee and which can become a big handicap of progress of this trial as we go along. Now, the Popovic Defence team, in anticipation of knowledge, confirmation, that they would be the first to -- they would be the ones to go first, have provided the Trial Chamber with a witness testimony schedule for the month of June. This was filed confidentially, and so I will not mention much more than I have. We wish to thank you, Mr. Zivanovic, for having done this in a timely fashion, but also because it opened our eyes to various problems which we wouldn't have been able to ask Mr. Cubbon to deal with during the 65 ter meeting. First of these problems is the expected testimony of Miladin Kovacevic. This is an expert witness. Now you have provided his report in the original language, which is the B/C/S. The translation of his report is not yet ready, at least to my knowledge, unless it was finalised yesterday. And you schedule this guy to testify on the 6th, between the 6th and the 9th of June. Mr. Cubbon asked you during the 65 ter meeting when you expect the translation to be ready. You said it's expected soon, but that Mr. Kovacevic could safely be moved to the second part of June if the translation is not ready soon. So I see you trying to stand up, anxious to give the information to the Trial Chamber, so I will stop here for the time being and see what information you can give us. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we moved his testimony for July, and you will be informed about it through our notice which will be filed today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in the meantime, what are you going to do with the days of the 6th and the 9th of June when you had anticipated to bring this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We make a schedule of our witness list and you will get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. It is also important because Mr. McCloskey, in the meantime, there is also another motion from the Popovic Defence team seeking to add, in relation to this witness, to add some more exhibits to the 65 ter list, and we enjoin you to come forward with your response to this motion at the earliest possible because ultimately it does have some bearing, albeit little, on when Mr. Kovacevic can be brought forward to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can tell you, having given this kind of notice, I'm not going to be objecting to a 65 ter list motion. If it's on the 65 ter list, no problem. Whether it's admissible or not that's the crux of it for me so I don't have a problem with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, can we decide it orally here and now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's proceed immediately with granting the motion. The motion was filed on the 21st of May by the Popovic Defence team, seeking an addition to the 65 ter list of Defence exhibits that are exclusively relevant to expert witness Miladin Kovacevic. The Trial Chamber has heard Mr. McCloskey for the Prosecution declaring that he -- the Prosecution has no objection to this, to the granting of this motion. The Trial Chamber therefore grants the motion and the Popovic Defence team is authorised to add the documents mentioned or attached to the motion to the 65 ter list accordingly. Now, what is the problem that we wanted to alert you to? And again, please try to understand that in dealing with this, we are not trying to be finicky, we are basing ourselves on past experience. In the present case, past experience is even more important because we are dealing with a -- not just one or two accused but seven accused with one Defence case coming immediately after or following immediately after the other. Without in any manner wanting to be interpreted as saying the following within a context of equality of arms or parity of arms between Prosecution and Defence, experience has taught us that a Defence team, albeit the most organised of all Defence teams, doesn't have behind it the structure that the Prosecution has. I know that the Tribunal offers all the assistance that is required to bring in witnesses and do whatever is necessary to procure the presence of witnesses here in The Hague, but not everything depends on the Tribunal. Much depends on how early you act, how long you cast your view in order to be able to plan properly, problems that could arise, such as, for example, bad planning on the team that has come before you, contingencies, you will I'm sure encounter problems, you will find witnesses that have promised to come over but which now have changed their mind and decide that they don't want to come over and they tell you this at the 11th hour. We have encountered such problems with the Prosecution, and irrespective of the fact that the Prosecution is perhaps better placed to deal with these problems, and irrespective of the fact that the Prosecution has got a better support structure at its disposal, we still encountered problems and there were days when we were faced with the following -- either of the following situations. "Your Honours, we are finishing with this witness earlier than expected, we are afraid we don't have any further witness for the remainder of the week." Or, "Your Honours, a witness who we intended to bring forward on Monday will not be coming and we can't make it in time to replace the witness with another." And all this is understandable. These are problems which unfortunately have arisen and which will continue to arise. If the Prosecution has found itself in the impossibility of finding a remedy to at least these two problems but there are also others, I'm sure that the Defence teams will not be in any better position. If anything, I think you will have more problems in trying to sort out these problems. And the bottom line is that you need to embark as from now on very careful planning, very careful planning. You have witnessed what has happened throughout this year and a half. We've had witnesses that were anticipated to last two days, three days, in the witness box giving evidence, and who lasted half the time, witnesses who lasted longer, and that is going to happen again, and there is no way we can forestall that and avoid it unless we fix a maximum time within which each testimony has to be concluded. But again, we have tried to be as flexible as we could with you and we've tried to impose as little time limits as possible. But we don't want that to be translated into time loss. I was going to say wasting of time but I prefer to use something more neutral because I'm sure that any such happening will not be intentional but it would just be accidental. So our responsibility is your responsibility. Together, we have a responsibility to show the utmost respect to those that created this Tribunal and who finance this Tribunal. There is no way we can remain passive to any loss unnecessary or unavoidable loss of -- avoidable loss of time. So we need to make an effort to move forward with the minimum possible loss of time. For this, you need to plan. For this, you need to plan. And you need to plan ahead because you may encounter problems with visa requirements, if a visa requirement is required by the Dutch authorities. You will recall we even had a problem with one witness coming here being returned to Kenya and having to come back again at major expense and costs to the Tribunal. We have a responsibility to try and avoid these things happening as much as possible. I'm not putting any blame on the Prosecution for that occurrence. The Prosecution had done everything within their power to get the witness here in time for his witness but it did not materialise. So you need to do this as an ongoing exercise. We very much enjoin you to do your utmost not to put us in a position where we come on any particular day and you tell us, "We are sorry, but the Dutch authorities," for example, "have not yet issued a visa to our witness." Yes, I know that you require to have an approximate date for the testimony of the witness before you can apply for a visa because the visa will be also limited in time but this is why you need to do very serious planning, very serious planning. We are telling you this because I'm sure that you would want to know that we are seriously concerned about this problem. We would love to hear any suggestions that you may have on this subject, but we have no words which are sufficient enough and strong enough to reflect well the concern that we have in our mind. We know that if you don't help yourselves in this, you will put the Trial Chamber in a position when it will have to intervene, when it will have to intervene. So forewarned is forearmed, but more than a warning, this is an exhortation to you all to do your utmost when it comes to planning, not to put the Trial Chamber in a position where it has to face a public criticism for losing time unnecessarily or which would be avoided. We'll have a 25-minute break now and we will reconvene afterwards. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Recapitulating and before we move to the next point, what we would require you to do, very briefly put, is that each one of you examines the revised list of witnesses, make sure at the earliest possible time, even tomorrow, if possible, of the availability when they are available because what we certainly want to avoid is coming here and finding an unpleasant surprise, which could be restricted or limited to one particular, the same Defence team, or could extend to the other Defence team. We don't want a situation where, for example, Mr. Zivanovic, all of a sudden decides that -- and this happens -- that it pays more his client to forget about the last two, three witnesses, for one reason or another, we wouldn't go into that, and renounces to those last two, three witnesses. What would be the consequence then? What we don't want is to come here the following day, with Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Meek, if he's still here, saying, "Sorry, we are not in a position to start our case before another two weeks because we were anticipating the Popovic Defence case to last two weeks longer." This is what you need to avoid and I think it requires cooperation amongst you, in other words team work, plus cooperation and careful planning. Now, I'm coming back to you, Mr. Zivanovic. You have -- you don't need to stand up. You have shown an indication that you will be requesting for two witnesses, at least, to testify via videolink. We enjoin you to file the necessary motion at -- it's filed already? Thank you. Because this requires time. In other words, they can't fix a videolink from one day to the other. And these two witnesses are scheduled to testify quite early in your Defence case, so you need to liaise with whoever will help you with the videolink, if the motion is granted, because we still have obviously to await the Prosecution response and decide, but on the assumption, just for argument's sake that it will be granted, you need to plan ahead. Missing expert reports you have dealt with already. I don't need to bring them up again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, Judge Kwon is rightly drawing to my attention that I should ask you, Mr. McCloskey, if you could possibly come back with your response to this motion in relation to videolink testimony the earliest possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We will try to get it this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. All right. Very soon we will be deciding the Popovic motion for certification following our decision granting the Prosecution motion to reopen its case, which you are aware. We will be handing down a decision, and according to what our decision will be, obviously you will need, Mr. Zivanovic, to together with the Prosecution, possibly come back to us with your proposal. I don't want to be interpreted as giving beforehand an indication of how we will be deciding the motion for certification but on the assumption again for argument's sake that we will, there is the question that we also hinted at when we handed down the decision granting the Prosecution motion, and we will do our utmost to ensure that a fair trial is secured. Okay. We are informed that in the course of the 65 ter meeting, a question arose as to what will be the correct procedure to be followed when expert witnesses are called and examined in chief by the party, by the Defence team that has produced such witness. We are told that there was a bit of an argument between the various Defence teams and the Prosecution, the Prosecution maintaining that the other Defence teams should first cross-examine the expert witness before the Prosecution is asked to cross-examine him or her, while the rest of the Defence teams took diametrically opposed position on this. It is already planned that one or more of these witnesses will be testifying very early into the Popovic Defence team, and we want this issue to be determined before we start. So our decision today, which we took yesterday, is to invite you to come forward with any submissions that you wish to make on this issue now, and that would put us in the position where we can either incorporate it in the guidelines that we will be issuing shortly or decide it separately, if it requires to be so decided. I do have an indication on who took part in the discussions during the 65 ter meeting. I don't want necessarily to limit myself to those of you who intervened. Would anyone of you wish to address the Trial Chamber? Mr. Bourgon? Of course, you will have an opportunity to address the Trial Chamber too, Mr. McCloskey, when it's over. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First, Mr. President, I would like to say that we believe that this issue affects not only expert witnesses but in fact all witnesses who will testify as part of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are correct, but the way it was put to us is that during the 65 ter meeting, it was rather limited to the evidence of expert witnesses. You are right, it applies across the board to all witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We take the view, Mr. President, as we mentioned during the Rule 65 ter meeting that cross-examination should begin with the Prosecution for the following reasons. Our most important justification for this is that we take the view that it will best favour the flow and the thorough presentation of the evidence before the Trial Chamber. We believe that the Prosecution will necessarily adopt a comprehensive approach to cross-examining any witnesses, bearing in mind that the Prosecution will cross-examine in the light of the evidence that a witness can bring against any of the co-accused in this case. That being the case, we think that this will significantly shorten any cross-examination by any of the co-accused that may follow thereafter. And this will of course save a lot of court time. Our main consideration here is that due to the exceptionally high number of co-accused in this case, this would make things much shorter and much more effective. Having the Prosecution go first will reduce the possibility of any overlap. Once the Prosecution has conducted its cross-examination of any witnesses, then the resulting cross-examination by any of the co-accused should be able to have to limit any overlap and should assist the Trial Chamber in controlling and limiting the resulting cross-examination. Another argument that militates in favour of having the Prosecution go first is to better protect the rights of the accused and I say this in light of the numerous, if I can call it this way, theories of Defence that co-exist amongst the co-accused in this case. So it is much better in our view to have the Prosecution go first and then have the co-accused take the second bite at the apple and terminate the cross-examination. For all these reasons, Mr. President, we believe that and we respectfully request that in your guidelines that will be issued for the presentation of the evidence during the Defence case, that we simply go, take the following approach, examination-in-chief, cross-examination by the Prosecution, and then cross-examination by the co-accused who wish and who may elect not to conduct any cross-examination once the Prosecution has done its work. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Anyone else wishes to address the Chamber? Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I completely agree with what my learned friend just said, what my colleague just said, and I would also like to add that to proceed this way could also make it so that the procedure will be faster and more efficient. It is quite possible that the Defence after the cross-examination led by the Prosecutor will request a recross-examination because obviously there will be things that will come across only during the cross-examination of the witness by the Prosecutor. So I believe in fact that this is the procedure that would be the most efficient and this procedure would protect the best the rights of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, Madam Fauveau. Any further contributions, submissions? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I do not agree with this approach. I think as we look at the expert witnesses, most of the experts will be experts that are not impacting adversely on the various accused. They will come at us with mostly a unified approach using each other's experts to attack the Prosecution's case which is normal and is what we expect and given that's the fact, the Prosecution should be able to see where each Defence is coming from so that I can respond finally after six examinations, seven -- six or seven examinations, I can respond to all of them in one shot as opposed to Mr. Zivanovic brings out one part of an expert that's for his case, I cross-examine, then Ms. Fauveau brings out another part, I'm going to be able to, I would think, recross on that so you're going to see me coming back and forth wanting to respond to each individual Defence that's brought up something new. I don't want to be in a position where I'm anticipating having to cross-examine on all subjects. That's not my style and it won't be the style of my team. We will be targeted to what we see the important points are that are brought out in direct examination or perhaps lying quietly in a report but I don't want to just design a cross-examination to include everything that each defendant might bring up. That would be an unreasonable burden to put on everyone because the cross-examinations would be much longer. I think the more reasonable way is they bring out what they need to bring out, I'll cross-examine on all of that, and of course, they can have, if there is some issue, then they can individually come back at the witness. And then it will hopefully be through at that point. But if we take this different approach, I may have to come back each time someone brings up something else. Now, if we had a situation where one expert hammered a co-accused, then we might want to take a little different approach for that co-accused, but I don't see that happening often. I think they are going to be unified effort and it's all going to be coming at the Prosecution so we should just respond to it one time. You don't want me jumping up and having to say, okay, I need to respond to that cross-examination, I need to respond to that one, that one, that one, and I will -- if it's a good cross-examination I will likely have to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Yes, Mr. Bourgon? Mr. Bourgon, while you prepare to reply to Mr. McCloskey, would you also like to address maybe what has already happened in the past when you had one expert witness who was a common expert and he testified here and the same issue arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, in my experience -- what happened in my experience, Mr. President, is that of course all examination-in-chief if it's a common expert witness then, of course, all examination-in-chief are done before the Prosecution does any cross-examination. To me that's not even an issue. The issue is when do you conduct the cross-examination? If two co-accused have different experts, and my experience has been in other cases that first the Prosecution will go and then the second accused would do the cross-examination. But I'm also informed that in other cases, the different approach was taken. So I don't think that there is a uniform approach before this Tribunal. I believe, Mr. President, what is important is that we have to look at the purpose of the cross-examination. It is either to attack the credibility of the witness or to attack the evidence that he can provide for the person who presented that witness. Now, if a co-accused does any cross-examination, we do it for the exactly same purpose of the Prosecution but, as a get-go, we are not the opposing party in this case and the Prosecution should go first and if there are any resulting issues, then the co-accused go at it. We think that this would save a lot of court time and make it much easier for the Trial Chamber to control the cross-examination time. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Bourgon. As I said -- yes, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think if the Court even at the beginning of the trial reconfirmed to us that each of the accused will be tried as if it was their separate case and the Rules certainly afford for that, and that's Rule 82, and if you look and follow the logic in my opinion of Rule 82 and that is an accused if he presents evidence certainly we wouldn't have an opportunity in other proceedings to cross-examine witnesses of other accused unless the case was joined. This case was joined. Prosecution has the ability and the wherewithal to cross-examine that witness. I think the approach that the Defence is suggesting is reasonable, I think it's it in accordance with the Rules. I don't see in the Rules anywhere that it suggests or supports the position of the Prosecution that we should, as the accused, be allowed or be even requested to cross-examine other accused's experts or witnesses. I'm being tried on this case separately from my co-accused. They can take a position adverse to me. It's what the Prosecution is charging me with that I'm most interested in, not what my fellow accused may have as their theory or charges that they may allege. I'm not answering those charges but putting us in a position to cross-examine first, certainly forces us to answer those charges as well. I think it's important to know what the Prosecution is going to do, his cross-examination should come first and it's absolutely in my opinion logical in accordance with the Rules and the Court should allow the Defence to follow the cross-examination of the Prosecution. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Do you wish to comment further, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just lastly it's my understanding the other -- the Prlic and Milutinovic trials do it the approach that I'm suggesting though I will try to confirm that. That will not be hard to confirm. But I don't -- it's not -- in reading the way the Court has always allowed the parties, you have always allowed us to deal with witnesses and bring up either cross or redirect on issues that have not been brought up before and so I would fully expect to you do that. If we do it the way they are planning that means whenever a new issue is brought up by a new cross-examination I will be allowed to respond and if I bring up something else, they will be allowed to respond. In that way, I'm jumping up and down all the time and that's just not going to work out practically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. And Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's conclude it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The example brought up by my colleague is simply something that in this case we have had this experience whereas there were some cross-examinations conducted, there was a cross-examination conducted by one of my colleagues which brought up some new areas, I tried to intervene after and I was not given the leave by the Trial Chamber because the issue had been dealt with before. So that example that my colleague is bringing forward I don't think is relevant. What matters is the evidence-in-chief is presented, the Prosecution does what it has to do to undermine either the credibility or the contents of the report, and if there is any resulting issues, then the co-accused do it and then we'll save significant court time. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. As I said earlier on, we'll come back to you with our decision which will be incorporated in the guidelines, decision or ruling that we will -- we intend to hand down or separately. Another topic that needs to be resolved and on which we do not intend to sit much further. On the 9th of this month, the Prosecution filed a confidential motion requesting us to order the Popovic Defence team to provide sufficiently detailed summaries of 12 of his proposed witnesses with a view to allowing the Prosecution to be in a position to adequately prepare for cross-examination. The Prosecution basically submits that these 12 witness summaries manifestly fail to comply with the requirements of Rule 65 ter and that -- the relevant jurisprudence on the matter and do not provide the Prosecution with adequate notice of the facts to which the witnesses will testify. Now, a few days later, on the 15th of May, Popovic and Pandurevic filed their responses. And on the 19th May, the Beara Defence team filed a motion joining the position taken by the Pandurevic Defence team. Now, we asked Mr. Cubbon to raise this matter during the 65 ter meeting which he did, and the -- you were invited to sit down, talk, negotiate if necessary, and try to find a solution without the need for Chambers to intervene in this matter. You were also asked that you will be expected to report back to the Trial Chamber today of the outcome of any discussions that may have taken place on this. So what we want to know is whether there is -- whether there have been discussions and whether there is an outcome that is worth hearing about. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic and I have had a chance to speak briefly on this topic. We both have fundamentally different views and his is held strongly, and he's made it very clear. I think the fundamental difference is that they have provided us some information of what the person is going to talk about, but nothing about the details. In many cases nothing about the details. And we need the details. And for an example, could we go into private session for a minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sure. Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, do you wish to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that we provided enough of information to the Prosecution through our Rule 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop there. Basically the conclusion is that there is no agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which means that we will be deciding the matter and it will be decided before we start with your Defence case. Yes, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, can we go back to private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go back into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't want to add too much. I did actually take it upon myself to try and broker some compromise here, I sent Mr. McCloskey an e-mail at 5.00 on Tuesday after our meeting but it didn't merit the courtesy of a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was bad timing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I looked with great interest at the Prosecution's filing the other day in which it was able, notwithstanding the inadequacy of the summaries to give pretty precise estimates for how long it's going to cross-examine all these witnesses and I really rather thought that gave the lie to the genuineness of this complaint. I would hope we can sort this out. I've spoken to Mr. McCloskey. As far as I'm aware he takes no issue with any of the summaries on my 65 ter list so I do not anticipate being the recipient of a motion of this sort, doubtless 14 days before I'm about to start my case. But this is a waste of time in my view. Where does it go? Let's suppose you do decide Mr. Zivanovic has got to improve his witness summaries a little bit and he does and that's still not to the Prosecution's liking. What do they then do? File another motion? Ultimately there is no sanction. We have got through this trial by dealing with questions of disclosure on an informal basis and if Mr. McCloskey has got things he needs to know from Mr. Zivanovic he can ask him and Mr. Zivanovic I'm sure will tell him and we can get on with hearing the evidence. My position, you know, on the merits of the motion is that you should not grant the Prosecution the relief it sought. They know every witness in this case very well. They've interviewed most of them. Very, very many of them have given evidence and there is nothing they don't know about what Mr. Krajisnik is about to say and they are thoroughly ready to cross-examine him and all the other witnesses in Mr. Zivanovic's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, I'm afraid our client is really feeling very, very unwell. He has been for much of the morning. And we would ask for a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Of course. Had you told us before we would have --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, we waited for him to indicate when he was really so unwell as to be able to continue. He's now done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In addition, if General Gvero prefers to go back to the Detention Unit, I think I can intervene to ensure that provided of course that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not at the moment, Your Honour. His general well-being is something that we were going to address on his behalf a little later in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But perhaps we could have a short break now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of how long, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would suggest 15 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will have a short break of 15 minutes and if you need more than that, Mr. Josse, will you come back to us, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Break taken at 11.38 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, General Gvero, good afternoon to you. THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] I believe that I shall be able to follow the proceedings to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We have every interest to make sure that you feel comfortable in the course of the proceedings. If at any time you need a break or you need to go back to the Detention Unit, we are here to help you. THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you very much for your interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Coming back to what we were discussing before the short break, our position is as follows, Mr. Zivanovic and Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Haynes and Mr. Beara for whatever it concerns you, I mean, it's -- our preference would be not to decide this issue and this is why we told you to try and sit down around a table and discuss. It's unfortunate that you have not come to an agreement. However, there may be a reason for that, and while we were sitting outside on the terrace waiting for the sitting to resume, we talked about it and we believe that if we give you an important guideline and invite you to have further talks, further discussions amongst yourselves, that could possibly be conducive to an agreement. And the guideline is the following, Mr. Zivanovic. We do not believe that the purpose of the Rule that applies is to obtain from you an indication of the subject matter that the witness will be testifying upon. That would not be enough. What is required from the Rule is more than that. What is required from the Rule is an indication of areas and facts that will be dealt with by the witness and possibly the manner in which they will be dealt with, if you are aware of that. So -- and you move from there. You move from there. It's true that the whole issue is plagued with problems and that is particularly why we would prefer you to come to an agreement rather than have us decide the issue.
