So we are inviting you to sit around a table again and discuss what applies to one witness may not apply to another and if you engage into a proactive discussion and exchange of ideas amongst yourselves, you would probably get a better result than if you put us in a position where we have to decide the issue ourselves. So we will be deciding the issue later on, if you don't come to an agreement. That is the position. Now, next item is -- there is very little I have to say about this, Rule 92 bis, 92 ter motions, the Beara problem we have dealt with already, but there is still the Popovic motion that requires a response from you, and since the Popovic Defence team will be first to go, we would appreciate, Mr. McCloskey, if you could come back to us with your response the earliest possible. It will allow Mr. Zivanovic to plan better and us to take stock of the situation and what to expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, no problem. The Popovic case is our biggest priority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. There is also a motion from the Beara Defence team, while we are at it, the Beara Defence team, I referred to it earlier on this morning, has filed a motion not to reduce the amount of witnesses but to add further witnesses to the 65 ter list, namely four additional witnesses. Unless you are in a position to give us your response to this today, we also enjoin you to come forward with your response the earliest possible, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Given that it's so early at this point, the Prosecution does not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the motion is granted, with the understanding, Mr. Ostojic, that these four witnesses will be included in the total exercise, the whole exercise, in a holistic manner, expecting from you a serious -- which I don't doubt -- a serious attempt to try and reduce the Defence, the Beara Defence case significantly. We've had the -- over the past two months, an exchange of motions, responses, replies, counter-motions, dealing with the correct meaning of the Serbo-Croat word "rukovodjenje," whether it means control as against managing. I think you are all aware of the exchange that has taken place. We are taking a position on this today, and we are informing you accordingly. We have a CLSS translation of Exhibit 407, Prosecution Exhibit 407 and Prosecution Exhibit 3032. And we are admitting the relative document as is. This will leave, of course, unprejudiced the issue of the correct translation of the Serbo-Croat word which I will try and repeat, "rukovodjenje." We will leave it unprejudiced, in other words, this will remain a matter for the forthcoming evidence. We are sure we are going to receive evidence on one version or one interpretation and other evidence on another interpretation. We'll hear what you have in store for us and then we will give due weight to what information we receive and decide later. In other words, for the time being, we are putting you on notice that we will not be deciding any of the motions and counter-motions that we have had on the subject matter. We believe that this is a matter that is best left to the evidence that we will be hearing in due course. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the event that it may simplify that is that the Prosecution's position is not that control is a term of command and so just to make that clear, and so the difference between control and management may be an interesting debate but we are -- have never suggested that control is a function, a direct function, of command. Just so that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I'm sure that your counterparts, your colleagues, on the Defence side will take that into consideration, even though it has already been stated in some of your filings. Now, during the 65 ter meeting, there was an issue that was raised by you, by the parties, rather than by Mr. Cubbon, and that is disclosure obligations under Rule 67. We are aware of the debate that took place and the respective positions taken by Prosecution and some of the Defence teams, particularly one Defence team, that's the Miletic Defence team. Yesterday, the Prosecution filed an urgent Prosecution motion for disclosure under Rule 67(A)(ii), basically Prosecution is requesting the Trial Chamber to order Defence counsel to provide full disclosure pursuant to Rule 67, the same subrule, no later than the 26th of May, 2008. There are two options. We either hear submissions that you may have today from the Defence teams in a brief manner, or else we will reduce the time limit within which you have available under the Rules for filing a written reply. I don't know what you prefer. Either of the two is fine with us. But this matter has to be decided because we are talking of a deadline that is pretty much near and we are running short of time. Madam Fauveau, I'm calling upon you, if you wish to address the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I can do it now, if this is convenient for the Chamber, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the Prosecution motion concerns paragraph 2, only to obtain documents applying Articles -- Rule 67(A)(ii), my objection will be also limited. The only objection I have for the moment is that it is about a matter of principle because as far as I'm concerned, all the statements of witnesses I have communicated to the Prosecution, according to this rule, Defence has the obligation to give one week before the presentation of its -- those declarations for the witnesses which are quoted and this is about the date, what is the date for the Defence? We consider that for General Miletic, we will start our own presentation, that is for General Miletic, we do not consider that the Defence of General Miletic will have the presentation of its case on 2 June but it will be the other one which begins. As for the prosecutors, this is only a matter of principle because we transmitted all the statements, it is only an objection concerning the date. Now, maybe I am jumping a bit the gun but if the Prosecution intends to put a motion by Rule 67(A)(ii), 67(A)(i) concerning copies of books, documents, which the Defence has or which can control, our position will be different and we will consider that this part of the Rule does not apply in the present case because it's unfavourable to the accused. The Article was modified during the case, during the trial, and since it is a Rule which is unfavourable to our client, we will oppose. If such a motion is put. I do not wish to develop and take more time now on this question because the motion of the Prosecution -- there is no motion of the Prosecution under 67(A)(i).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would help us to know how you consider it adverse to the accused when it's limited to pieces of evidence that is intended to be brought into the record, because you see that copies of statements, if any, of all witnesses whom the Defence intends to call to testify at trial, and copies of all written statements, et cetera, which the Defence intends to present at trial. Copies of, et cetera, how does it become prejudicial to --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't consider that part of the Rule is unfavourable. It's the reason why I said that as far as paragraph 2, my objection is only about the date, but if the Prosecution intends to present another motion, in that case, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as we can all tell from this motion, this motion does not require the Prosecution -- or this Rule does not require, nor anticipate, the Prosecution has to file a motion. It says the Defence shall. The only reason we filed the motion for (ii) in this case is because we got fair indication from them that they weren't going to provide us with statements and in fact there were many statements we didn't have. I had assumed they would be following (i) and that hadn't become a problem yet, but I will amend my motion verbally now to include (i) for them to provide documents if that's what it's going to take, I see she has made her position clear on that. I didn't think I would have to file a motion on that but I obviously do. It's not of course true for all accused but it is -- it is something that should be worked out at this point. I think it will solve problems later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Madam Fauveau? And I also -- do you wish to address the Chamber, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I think it might be convenient if I do it now. I know what my obligations are under these Rules. And I have every intention of complying with them. And I don't see what basis has been raised by the Prosecution for the making of an order against Defence counsel that they shall apply with their lawful obligation under the Rules. This motion has absolutely no basis whatsoever. The date for compliance has not yet passed. It would be quite another thing if the Prosecution were coming here and saying, Mr. Haynes has failed to disclose material which we know he has. But there is no basis for the Prosecution to apply for and for you to make an order that the Rule shall be complied with. There is no basis for suggesting I'm going to break the Rules. This is completely ahead of the gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Madam Fauveau? And then you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, because of the answer of the Prosecution, I would like briefly to say why I feel that this modification of the Rule concerning the little A is disfavourable to the Defence. First of all, for me, it's not very clear, I don't see what this Rule actually refers. If it's documents which we will present during examinations, direct examinations, those of 65 ter, of course we have an obligation to disclose to the Prosecution, that's what we have already done. On the other hand, if it's about the documents which we intend to use during other examinations or other witnesses of the Defence, this Rule then clearly is disfavourable to our client because the Prosecution has no such obligation, and in this procedure will be using this during the examination. So they will have presented their own argument about documents which were not communicated to us and if this Rule is applied to the Defence as it is written here, and if it has to subsume all the documents for the Defence at any stage of the proceedings, then one may wonder whether the Prosecution did disclose all the documents which he intends to use in these proceedings, in particular during the counter-examination, cross-examinations of our witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. President, to join the opposition to the motion by my colleague Mr. Haynes but also to add that the motion in our view is premature. However, the timing might be right and the guidelines that the Trial Chamber will issue to confirm that the Prosecution should give us ahead of time any documents they intend to use in cross-examination of our witnesses. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Beara Defence team agrees and we join.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. So we will decide that in due course. Yes, Mr. Haynes -- Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's my understanding that some Defence counsel feel that this Rule doesn't even apply because it was enacted after the Prosecution started. We are getting very close to the beginning of the Popovic case, we don't have the statements from him, so this Rule is ripe in the case of the first accused, and this week time-limit that is suggested is a bare minimum and that I would of course ask you to consider that we get material prior to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We enclosed all our statements to our motions, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you making a statement to the effect that both under the first paragraph and -- in other words -- and the second paragraph, there is no further documents that need to be disclosed? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is my -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have just a CD with the [indiscernible] attached to the report of Mr. Miladin Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you had a request by the Prosecution to inspect and copy any books, documents, photos that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't got any specific request for any documents, book or anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's not my practice to bring up e-mails but I do -- I did make a Rule 67 request to everyone and I do have some 92 bis statements from Mr. Zivanovic, and the Kovacevic statement but as for some of these witnesses, many of them I have no statement and if there is no statement then I would hope to be told that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's -- you have a responsibility under the Rules, Mr. Zivanovic, we are not here to preach what your responsibilities or duties are. Make sure that they are all observed because there will be consequences otherwise, as there were in other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the request you made is based on Rule 67(A)(ii), not 67(A)(i) which provides for the inspection by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will have to go look at my e-mail, if it was done properly I would have asked for both. Actually it's right here so I'll be able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I asked for 67(A) which would include both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Inspection by the Prosecution of the documents which is in custody of the Defence for the use at the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. This is a request pursuant to Rule 67(A) that you provide to the Prosecution copies of all statements of all witnesses whom you intend to give evidence at trial including live witnesses, 92 bis, quater. We also request that we be allowed to inspect and copy any books, documents, photographs, intangible objects -- sorry, I'm sure I'm going too fast -- in your custody or control which are intended for use as evidence at trial. Alternatively, if it's more convenient, you can provide us with copies of this material. And it goes on. And that was 10 April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Independently of the principle which may or may not be involved that Madam Fauveau referred to what I suggest is this, Mr. Zivanovic, if you could follow what I'm saying, I'm saying that irrespective of the principle and the rest of the debate on whether there is a principle and to what extent and how it should be applied and whether the Prosecution motion is a timely one or not, I mean, bypassing all these issues, what I suggest is that now that the matter has been raised, why don't you sit down again with Mr. McCloskey and should there be other material that may or should have been disclosed and hasn't been disclosed or material that Mr. McCloskey wants to have access to pursuant to either the first or the second paragraph, that you try to thrash this in an orderly manner. I see that in this issue there is good faith on both sides, there is not a question of someone trying to evade one's responsibility. This is not the case. So what I suggest is that you sit down together and try to thrash this out. In the meantime, the rest of the issues can be postponed and will be decided if there is an ad hoc request for the matter to be decided. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to be misunderstood by the Chamber, by the Prosecution. As far as General Miletic, we don't have other documents than those which any way are in the e-court -- electronic disclosure system but I think this Rule should not apply if maybe somebody has another document but there is another Rule, Article -- Rule 66(B) which gives the same obligation to disclose to the Prosecution but only on the request of the Defence. So I'm sure that, at the moment this case was prepared, several teams of Defence elected not to make this request because there was no obligation. Now we have this obligation and this puts us in an unfavourable position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But in the meantime I think the matter can be dealt with in the way suggested because what's urgent about it is the Popovic Defence case. If there is a need to go deeper into the matter and decide it from the legal aspect or from some other aspect of course we will do that later on but in the meantime we need to be practical and pragmatic in our approach and what I have suggested I think should be stomached well by the Prosecution and Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just like to say that the -- it is our position that the contents of Rule 67(A)(i) has been rendered moot by Rule 65 ter. Any documents that we had that we intend to use were put on our list and were given to the Prosecution. If we find something else between now and the witness appearing, of course we will give it to the Prosecution. We are fulfilling our obligations. This 67(A)(i) has been rendered moot. As for the other one, we are in contact with the Prosecution and we are disclosing our statements in the same manner. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That may well be the case, Mr. Bourgon, but let's see whether these will be pleasures yet to come in which case we will not shy away from deciding the issue. The only other things we have on our agenda, is the state of health of the accused and basically nothing else, unless you wish to raise any other matter arising from the 65 ter meeting or independently of and beyond or beyond the 65 ter meeting. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, the issue that we wish to raise and which we alluded to earlier really does relate to our client's well-being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to deal with this in open session or in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In open session, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the reason we want to put this on record is that it may have a consequential impact on this trial and we felt it appropriate to mention it at this Pre-Defence Conference. General Gvero was very grateful to the Trial Chamber in granting his application for provisional release. It goes without saying that I'm instructed to emphasise that he was bitterly disappointed by the ultimate decision of the Appeals Chamber reversing the period of release that had previously been granted to him. His lawyers, Your Honours, of course appreciate that there is nothing that can be done about that by this Trial Chamber. And we have explained that to our client. He fervently believes that the standards, that is the law, in effect, in relation to this particular issue, has changed and putting it colloquially, it's his view that the goal posts have changed during the course of this trial and that has affected him in a number of ways and I repeat, he is bitterly disappointed about the end result. He feels in effect that he's been caught in a trap because having voluntarily surrendered, he initially faced an indictment with simply two other men, and he anticipated a relatively short trial. He was then joined to the five other men who now sit with him in the dock of this Court. That of course had a consequential setback in terms of the time this trial was going to take. He was of the view that that setback was greatly compensated by the fact that hitherto, he had regular periods of provisional release which was important to him for a number of obvious reasons, not least for his general well-being. He has spent the last three months, like his six co-accused, I'm bound to say in passing, in custody. He is in extremely low spirits, not to say upset. Commenting on that, it's an obvious comment, of course he had the anticipation that he thought he was going to be released although he knew that the appeal was pending. He hoped the appeal decision would go his way, it didn't, and it has literally put him into a state of some despair, frankly. For the most part Mr. Krgovic has been dealing with that, being the B/C/S speaker in our team. General Gvero, prior to today's episode, had asked me to say that he is extremely concerned that he will be able to follow this trial on a daily basis. He certainly gave the appearance today of being unwell and in the end the trial was for a short period of time disrupted. The prospect of this trial lasting well into the future, as now appears the case based on the various 65 ter submissions that the Trial Chamber has received, is one that clearly concerns him and his lawyers greatly. He is, to state the obvious, 70 years of age. He's the oldest accused presently on trial at this Tribunal. As I am aware, the Trial Chamber knows that he suffers from various different ailments and illnesses and he takes a considerable amount of medication to try and ease those. Where this leads, Your Honour, apart from the fact that he's asked me to make this clear to the Trial Chamber and we are grateful that the Trial Chamber, in effect, wanted to hear about the well-being of each of the accused and in that guise I'm making this submission as well, but where it leads is, as best it can, we can only ask the Trial Chamber to take this into account in it's scheduling considerations in the coming weeks and months. He will do his best, that is our client, to follow this trial, to be here on a daily basis but he is concerned and he is in a very low state of well-being at the moment because of the reasons that I've alluded to and this Trial Chamber are only too well aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Does -- do you wish to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have no objection to moving his case up front and making -- there are arrangements that can be made for people that are not well, that are in the jail, as we know from other cases but we have no objection to moving it up front, if he wants to get it going, we'll go with him on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He will still have to await the outcome of the other trial -- the whole trial anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't think that would be a remedy at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, your words were words of wisdom, and as I made it clear already, we will certainly take into account -- take them into account. We of course agree with you completely that the present situation as it arises is what it is. However, that's what the circumstances are now. They can change. And if they change, of course, we will take that change into consideration and take whatever decisions may become necessary, but for the time being, you appreciate that the situation that you are faced with is the situation that we have. But we will, of course, take into account the concerns that your client has and that you have so capably aired.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We, that is his lawyers, really do understand that. I'm sure that General Gvero does as well, Your Honour. He realises that the situation, as Your Honour rightly puts it, is the situation that we face and there is nothing very much that can be done about it but I'm sure your words will be of some comfort and I hope support to him in the time to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. Does anyone else wish to address the Chamber on health issues? All right. Do you wish to address the Chamber on anything else, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It's about the scheduling. We have been informed that the recess this summer will be two weeks, and discussing first about the conference 65 ter, I did not ask for an extra week. I certainly said that we have somebody -- we have several teams for the Defence who will be preparing their case, and some of us mean we will have no holidays at all. After this conference, discussing with other colleagues, I think even with the Prosecutor, I'm not saying that he was in agreement with me, I feel that everybody thinks that two weeks is much too short and that indeed having only two weeks, this might cause more problems than advantages because I think that indeed it's very important to be well prepared and it is also necessary to be in a position at least to have a little pause because it's true that we have three months now to prepare the 65 ter lists, but I have to own up that as far as I'm concerned, me and my team, we have had practically no vacation during that period, in particular for the team who was working in the field practically all the time. Therefore what I would like to request is to take into consideration whether it wouldn't be possible to have three weeks this summer or another solution, I'm not quite sure how this could be done, how will this trial continue, are we going to continue on the same basis during the evidence, presentation of evidence by the Prosecution, or every four weeks will we have one week for a pause or? I will be extremely grateful if you could give us some indication. Other solutions, as far as I'm concerned, and some of my colleagues think is maybe too complicated. Really, it has to be only two weeks in August which I understand because of other considerations which you have to take into account, would it be possible to finish a week before on a Thursday and to start the trial on a Tuesday? Because this would then allow us to have a little more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, anyone else? Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I had assumed we would have had three weeks, that we were going to get a week at the other end of August, and in looking at the e-mails I see that I am wrong, so I would join Ms. Fauveau's request for a -- the length, the normal length, of the summer break. And she made brief reference to the fact that in the Prosecution's case, the Court took regular breaks for us to be able to organise our case and adjust and I just want to emphasise how critically important those breaks were for the Prosecution to be able to do just that, to help organise the number of witnesses that were coming, and to have a time where -- both an end time where they would be finished and a beginning time where they would start again. That was absolutely essential for us with the number of witnesses we had to put on to make this as smooth-running as we could. It also, as you know, was very helpful for everyone to have some break and I think in the long run, this has been a much more smooth-running trial than it would have been without that break which was initiated as you know by the Court originally and fully agreed to and worked out very well, I think, on all accounts, and I think this is one issue that everyone in the room agrees with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Anyone else? I suppose your silence means you agree with Madam Fauveau. You don't need to stand up. I mean, I take it that you all agree. The position is as follows. First of all, you may have been informed by Mr. Cubbon that we think there should be two days in July when we will not sit, namely the 17th and 18th of July. We have revised that. We will be sitting on those two days, the 17th and the 18th of July, but we will not be sitting on the 14th and the 15th of July. So I would like you to make a note of that. Our problem is the following, and before I try to explain it, let me assure you that we have not made our minds on this, except insofar as the -- we have a scenario that we haven't created ourselves, but a scenario that has -- presents itself as a result of the 65 ter filings, which basically means that for examination-in-chief alone, we are talking of 420 hours. Add to that the time, giving a conservative estimate of 50/50, which would be required for cross-examination, we are in the region of 1.000 hours because in addition to the Prosecution cross-examination, we have to allow also for cross-examination amongst the various Defence teams, plus time required for procedural issues and there will be several and a little bit of time which we usually take ourselves. That is alarming. And I hope you will agree with me that that scenario creates problems for us, creates multiple problems. We want to ensure that each one of you will have full opportunities to present your respective case, Defence case, adequately, according to due process laws and that there is a fair trial throughout. That is a concern that we have, something that we believe in, and I'm sure that in that we are on the same level. At the same time, we cannot allow a situation to obtain where you had already consumed, used, over 400 -- 466 hours in cross-examination during the Prosecution case, another 420, a conservative estimate because it could go beyond that, for the examination-in-chief, plus time that you are entitled to cross-examine the other Defence witnesses and experts. It's a difficult scenario and we would like you to appreciate that we are not happy with the situation. It is definitely our intention, Mr. McCloskey, that if this trial has run smoothly, we will do our utmost, with your help, to continue making it so. We do understand and appreciate and some people in the public or elsewhere who may have -- keep a watchful eye on the Tribunal might think otherwise, that the three months that we have had between the end of the Prosecution case and the beginning of the Defence case, has not been a holiday for any of you. You bombarded us with motions that we had to decide. None of us could take a break, a decent break, because of precisely of the amount of motions. That meant that you were working, in addition you were doing your investigative work in order to compile your list of witnesses, interview them and prepare. We are fully aware of this. And we have no intention to make things worse. Three months have been made use of. To an extent, they have produced results. They have not however produced the results that we had hoped for. You may not see it the same way we do. But that's the way we see it. And therefore, we need to meet halfway, to ensure that the scenario that we see ourselves working in is such that would allow us to take into consideration, to take into stock, your complaints and your desires. You will understand that the scenario becomes complicated, for example, because when I look at these tables and these calculations, even with all good intentions and expectations that each one of you will succeed in reducing your respective Defence cases, still I get statements like the one I got from Mr. Haynes earlier on this morning, that -- to the effect that he expects, and Mr. Haynes is not one lawyer who just throws statements without any -- having given them serious thoughts before, but he suggests that he thinks, he believes, that he will be starting his Defence case approximately before the end of this year. And my question is: Are you prepared, all of you, to make a commitment that by the end of this year, or latest end of January, all the seven Defence cases will be over and done with, will be finished? Because if you're prepared to make such a statement, then perhaps the language that I am using, the approach I'm taking, will also change. I know that you are going to work on this idea of trying to reduce the Defence case each one of you has been working so hard upon. So the position I am taking, after having consulted with my colleagues and having also seen the tentative chart -- not chart, table or schedule that you have presented us with, is that we are prepared to give it a very serious thought. We don't want to draw blood from anyone. We know that at the end of the day, you can take the horse to the stream but you can't make the horse drink. So our position is that we will do our utmost to try and accommodate you as problems become acute, and they are bound to become acute as we go along, but at the moment, not knowing exactly where we stand with you, and having this sort of confusion in our mind that on one side we have an estimate of hundreds and hundreds of hours, possibly total of 1.000 hours, at the same time someone saying that he hopes, and he is the last one to go, that he will be ready to go and should be going end of this month [sic], that's all very confusing to us. We need more information. We need to have the situation crystallise in the clearest way possible, and then you will have a response from us which we hope will be conducive to a continuation of the case in a smooth and respectful and practical pragmatic manner that we have endeavoured to keep it so far. There are problems and the problems need to be solved. We are not in a position to solve these problems on our own. We can of course impose deadlines, we can impose, we can cut down on the number of witnesses, we have all the powers that I referred to you -- referred you to earlier on during today's meeting. Our preference would be for you to see more sense into the issue. This is not a problem that we have brought on ourselves ourselves, but it's a problem that we are not blaming you for because presumably each one presented and organised, planned, the Defence case independently of others and not necessarily knowing the expected length of cases of others. Some of you have been extremely reasonable but that doesn't apply across the board. We expect further news from you, and then we decide. As far as the summer recess is concerned, I was noticing, studying this this morning, here there isn't an indication to extend the two weeks into three weeks, as was planned originally. Here, in the suggested schedule, the summer recess runs from the 4th up to and inclusive of the 15th of August which would mean resuming on the 18th of August. I don't think we will be able to move on that. I don't think we will be able to move on that. But if we see improvement, significant improvement, in the scenario that I have been referring to, of course we are prepared to discuss further with you and see where we can fit in breaks when they are really needed, and if they are needed. One thing that I disagree with Mr. McCloskey about is that it's one thing talking of one Prosecution case that starts and continues. Here we have seven Defence cases. So although it is true that while the Popovic Defence case is on, the other Defence teams are going to be engaged, they are not going to be engaged the same way you were engaged all the way when you were dealing with your case. There is a difference. They will be engaged and of course everyone needs a break, but for the time being, please don't ask us to be categoric and give you a straightforward answer, if and to what extent, and when, we would be granting any breaks. We need to move ahead. We need to move ahead in a fair manner, which will guarantee you your full rights, not under -- not just under the Statute and under the Rules but under international human rights law, which we can guarantee you all the way. All right. So the sooner you can come back to us with what the situation is more like the situation is going to be, and the sooner we are in a position to determine the Rule 92 bis and 92 ter motions that will -- that are already in place and will be forthcoming, the sooner we will be able to tell you when we can have a rest, which I'm sure will be well deserved because you are a hard-working lot and the way you have managed to keep us busy during these three months is remarkable, and also indicative that you haven't been sleeping or idling, you have been working, you have been working hard. Thank you. Is there any other matter that you would like to raise? There being none, I bring this Pre-Defence Conference to an end. On the 2nd of June, we will start with your Defence case. Be prepared with your opening statement, Mr. Zivanovic, and also your first witness. One thing I wanted to make sure, there are no protective measures in place for your -- for Krajisnik, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, because Mr. Haynes mentioned him in open session and I want to make sure that we were not doing something irregular. At the same time, please also make all your arrangements to make sure that he is available for evidence and have other witnesses in line present here in The Hague should, as I expect, his testimony last shorter than you think, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is for Krajisnik, for Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know right now, because I have to meet him this week or next week, and then I will be able to give a more accurate estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have his undertaking that he will be giving evidence. I hope you have that already. Because if you don't have, you need to prepare for that eventuality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I meant earlier on. So do you wish to make further submissions? Thanks. And Mr. Zivanovic and Mr. McCloskey, please try to meet on the outstanding issues that you have. We would very much appreciate if you put us in a position where we don't have to give certain decisions that are best left undecided. Okay? Thank you. And good afternoon to everybody.
